title: Seqlen spillover batcher: soft-capacity bucketing and padding-aware scheduling
author: Priya Nambiar
description: Motivation: existing seqlen bucketing approaches reduce padding but can create hard bin boundaries that underutilize batch capacity when workloads have heavy-tail length distributions or bursty short/long mixes. This PR introduces a 'spillover' batching heuristic that treats buckets as soft-capacity containers: short sequences preferentially join short-length buckets, but when a bucket is near capacity we allow low-cost spillover into adjacent buckets if the incremental padding cost is below a computed threshold. The goal is to reduce wasted token work while keeping per-request latency SLOs stable. Key changes: 1) Soft-capacity buckets: each bucket has a target capacity and a spill tolerance ratio. If accepting an extra request increases total padded-tokens by less than tolerance*expected_gain, the scheduler will allow spillover. 2) Padding-cost estimator: a lightweight estimator that computes incremental padded tokens for merging two sequences into a bucket; uses sequence length histogram + recent-runtime kernel efficiency model to convert padded tokens into an expected GPU-time cost (so we account for kernel selection and sequence-length-specific kernel scaling). 3) Kernel-aware routing: the runtime now tags candidate batches with preferred kernel flavor (fp16/quantized/packed attention) based on the highest-common-capability of included sequences; the scheduler prefers batch compositions that map to a single efficient kernel instead of mixing incompatible sequences. 4) KV-cache affinity hinting: when a request has a warm KV-cache (prefix match), it gets an affinity score that biases the scheduler to group it with others sharing the prefix to reuse KV memory and reduce duplicate KV loads. 5) Partial-flush thresholds for continuous batching: introduces a sliding flush threshold that permits earlier flushes for buckets with high variance to avoid p95 spikes while still allowing longer accumulation for low-variance buckets. 6) Config flags and observability controls: new runtime flags (spillover_enabled, spill_tolerance, kernel_affinity_weight, kv_affinity_weight, bucket_flush_sensitivity) and metrics (spillovers/second, padded_tokens_saved, kernel_switch_penalties, kv_affinity_hits). Implementation notes: this change touches the batcher, scheduler, and the kernel selection contract but keeps the public API unchanged. The algorithm is conservative by default (spillover_enabled=false) and gated behind a feature flag. Testing: unit tests for the padding estimator and bucket scoring, integration tests that simulate mixed-length workloads with mock kernels, and end-to-end CI runs on a small GPU harness. Performance: in internal perf lab tests on g4dn.12xlarge with a mixed workload (40% <64, 40% 64-512, 20% >512) we observed a 12.7% mean throughput increase and a 9.3% reduction in padded tokens for steady-state traffic; p95 latency improved by 6ms in steady-state and remained within SLO under burst scenarios. Rollout plan: feature gated + gradual rollout on Dedicated clusters: Canary -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% with automatic rollback on increased p95 or error rate. Backcompat: scheduler config is additive; no customer-facing changes unless flags are enabled. Follow-ups: 1) tune spill tolerance per model using Optimize heuristics, 2) expose a per-deployment dashboard for spillover metrics, 3) explore machine-learned cost model to replace the current estimator.

review_comments: Ethan Park: Overall looks solid; main concern is the cost-estimator accuracy under quantized kernels — can we add a calibration job?
Author (Priya): Added calibration harness in benchmarks/ci and a follow-up entry in the PR description; estimator exposes a calibration hook.
María Gonzalez: Suggest lowering default spill_tolerance to 0.05 for canary; also please add metrics for spillover-caused kernel switches.
Author (Priya): Set default to 0.05 and added kernel_switch_penalties metric, updated tests to assert the metric emits on switches.
Leo Zhang: KV affinity looks promising; risk is memory churn if we co-locate very large prefix caches. Can we cap affinity bonus by KV memory impact?
Author (Priya): Added kv_affinity_memory_penalty and unit tests that simulate large prefix cache scenarios; kept conservative defaults.
